content: The Sandbox tree, scientifically known as Hura crepitans (synonym Hura brasiliensis Wild), is an evergreen species belonging to the spurge family (Euphorbiaceae). It is native to the tropical regions of North and South America, particularly in the Amazon Rainforest. This tree is easily identifiable by its smooth brown bark, which is covered with numerous dark, pointed spines. These spines have earned it the nickname Monkey no-climb, as they make the tree difficult to scale. The Sandbox tree can grow to an impressive height of up to 100 feet (approximately 30 meters). Its large, ovate leaves can reach a width of up to two feet. The tree is monoecious, meaning it produces both male and female flowers on the same individual. The male flowers are found on elongated spikes, while the female flowers are solitary and grow in the axils of the leaves. The flowers are red in color and lack petals. The fruit of the Sandbox tree is a large capsule that exhibits explosive dehiscence. When the fruit ripens, it splits apart with a loud, explosive sound, forcefully ejecting its seeds to distances of up to 100 meters (328 feet). This dramatic dispersal mechanism has led to the tree being colloquially referred to as the Dynamite tree. The Sandbox tree thrives in wet soil and can tolerate a range of light conditions, from partial shade to full sun. It is often cultivated for its ability to provide shade. The tree's milky, caustic sap has been historically used by fishermen to poison fish, taking advantage of its toxic properties. Additionally, the wood of the tree, marketed under the name hura, is utilized in the production of furniture. Interestingly, Hura crepitans is also an ingredient in certain preparations of the hallucinogenic brew Ayahuasca, which is traditionally used in spiritual and medicinal practices in some South American cultures.
